points.title: Putting two complete ideas into one sentence with and, but, or and so

point_json.grammar_name: Coordination with and, but, or and so

teach.can_do: I can put two complete ideas into one sentence and show how the second one relates to the first.
teach.why_it_matters: Without these four words every sentence stops after one idea, and your reader is left to work out the joins on your behalf.
teach.meaning: A complete idea is a group of words you could put a full stop after and walk away: the fare went up. English lets you put two of them inside one sentence, but not by parking them next to each other. A joining word goes between them, and each one makes a different claim about the join. And adds. But turns. Or offers a choice. So gives the result. The two ideas stay equal in weight; neither is squeezed inside the other.

form.pattern: complete idea + , + and / but / or / so + complete idea
notes: The comma goes in front of the joining word, never after it.
When both ideas are very short the comma can be dropped: the gates opened and the queue moved.
One joining word per join. Two of them is always one too many.
form.negative: Each idea goes negative on its own: the ferry did not run, and the bus was not diverted.
form.question: Questions join in the same way: did the fare rise, or did the service simply get worse?

left.role: idea one, complete on its own
left.text: the fare went up in April

right.role: idea two, complete on its own
right.text: passenger numbers fell within a month

spec.caption: Two things that could each be a sentence, held together by one word: and, but, or, so.

worked_example.sentence: The council added two evening buses, but the last one still leaves before the late shift ends.
worked_example.why_this_form: The second idea works against the first, so the join has to be but. And would tell the reader that the two facts point the same way.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: With so, the sentence would claim the early departure is the result of adding the buses, which is not what happened.

notice_set.sentence: The station car park was full, so we left the car at home.
notice_set.question: Why did they leave the car at home?
options: Because the car park was full
notice_set.why: So marks whatever follows it as the result of what came before it.

notice_set.sentence: We arrived early, but the car park was already full.
notice_set.question: Did arriving early help?
notice_set.why: But warns you that the second idea works against the first, so early was not early enough.

notice_set.sentence: You can buy a ticket at the machine, or you can pay the driver.
notice_set.question: How many ways of paying are there?
notice_set.why: Or lays two possibilities side by side and lets the reader take either.

notice_set.sentence: The lift was out of order and the stairs were closed for cleaning.
notice_set.question: Do the two facts pull in the same direction?
notice_set.why: And simply adds. It makes no claim beyond both things being true.

notice_set.sentence: The service was cut in 2019, so the village lost its only link to the hospital.
notice_set.question: Which idea is the result?
notice_set.why: So always puts the result second. Everything after it happened because of what came first.

teach.rule_line: Two complete ideas in one sentence need a joining word between them.
teach.false_rule: That a comma on its own is enough to hold two complete ideas together. A comma cannot do that job; it needs one of these four words beside it.

errors.wrong: The bus service was cut, many villages now have no way of reaching the hospital.
errors.right: The bus service was cut, so many villages now have no way of reaching the hospital.
errors.why_it_happens: The two facts belong together and the comma feels like the mark for that. Nobody has told the learner that a comma can separate things but cannot join them.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: so.

errors.wrong: The fare went up in April passenger numbers fell within a month.
errors.right: The fare went up in April, and passenger numbers fell within a month.
errors.why_it_happens: The sentence was written in one breath and the seam between the two ideas was never heard. It happens most in the second half of a timed answer, when nobody is reading back.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: and.

errors.wrong: The fare went up, however the service did not improve.
errors.right: The fare went up, but the service did not improve.
errors.why_it_happens: However means what but means, so it is put where but would go. The two words mean the same thing and belong to different grammatical classes, and only one of them can sit next to a comma.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: however becomes but.

errors.wrong: Commuters wanted cheaper fares and to have more frequent trains.
errors.right: Commuters wanted cheaper fares and more frequent trains.
errors.why_it_happens: The second item is thought of as a separate wish and comes out with its own verb attached. And demands two things of the same shape, and nothing warns the learner when the shapes drift apart.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: to have.

pays_in.note: Every body paragraph needs at least one join a reader can trust.
pays_in.model: The scheme cut journey times, but it did nothing for the villages beyond the ring road.

pays_in.note: Any answer longer than one sentence hangs on these four words.
pays_in.model: I cycle in most days, so I only really use the train in winter.

pays_in.note: But and so tell you whether the next clause agrees with the last one or overturns it.
pays_in.model: The trial ran for three years, but the findings were never acted on.

used_in.quote: The answer is a chain of small consequences, and every link in it is one of these four words.
A two-clause answer sounds like a person talking; two one-clause answers sound like a form being filled in.

payload.sentence: The last train was cancelled, so we stayed the night in Marlow.
payload.question: Why did they stay the night?

feedback.why_key: So points forwards to the result, so everything after it happened because of the cancelled train.
feedback.feed_forward: Read so as and because of that.

payload.sentence: The reservoir refilled over the winter, but the hosepipe ban stayed in place.
payload.question: Was the ban lifted when the reservoir refilled?

feedback.why_key: But warns you that the second idea works against the first, so the refilling did not bring the ban to an end.
feedback.feed_forward: Read but as a warning that the direction is about to change.

items.decision_cue: the retail park, the old square

payload.context: From a first draft about town centres.
payload.sentence: The market moved to the retail park, the old square emptied within a year.
reasons: two complete ideas are held together by nothing but a comma
the second idea is not complete
the comma is in the wrong place
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Both halves could take a full stop and stand alone. A comma on its own cannot hold them; a joining word has to be there too.
feedback.feed_forward: Cover the comma and ask whether each side could be a sentence.

payload.context: From a report on a new park-and-ride site.
payload.stem: The car park opened in March, ___ the buses did not start running until June.

feedback.why_key: The second fact undercuts the first: the site was there and useless. But is the only one of the four words that says that.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the second idea helps the first or blocks it.

payload.context: Two neighbours talking on the stairs.
payload.stem: The lift has been broken since Friday, ___ I have been carrying the shopping up six floors.

feedback.why_key: The carrying is what the broken lift caused, and so is the word that marks a result.
feedback.feed_forward: If the second idea is the consequence, reach for so.

payload.context: Build one sentence about the Marlow depot.

expected: the depot closed in 2019 so forty drivers lost their jobs

feedback.why_key: The cause comes first and the result follows so. Swap them over and the sentence claims the drivers closed the depot.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the cause in front of so and the consequence after it.

payload.given: The library now opens on Sundays. Very few students use it.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that keeps both facts and shows that the second works against the first.

expected: now opens on sundays but very few students use it
now opens on sundays, but very few students use it

feedback.why_key: One sentence now carries the good news and the disappointment, and but is what tells the reader which is which.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the joining word by asking which way the second idea pulls.

payload.audio_text: We'd finished the shift, so we didn't wait for the late bus.

expected: we'd finished the shift so we didn't wait for the late bus
we had finished the shift so we did not wait for the late bus
wed finished the shift so we didnt wait for the late bus
we'd finished the shift so we did not wait for the late bus

feedback.why_key: In ordinary speech so is one quick unstressed syllable, and a listener who misses it writes two sentences where the speaker said one.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a small joining word at the seam between two ideas.

payload.context: From a paragraph on hospital waiting times.
payload.stem: Patients want shorter waits ___ clearer information about their appointments.

feedback.why_key: Two things of the same kind are being listed, and and is the word that adds without claiming anything else.
feedback.feed_forward: Use and when the second idea neither turns nor follows from the first.

items.decision_cue: April, the queues moved

payload.sentence: The charge came in last April, the queues moved to the ring road within a fortnight.

feedback.why_key: Both halves are complete sentences, so the comma needs a joining word beside it or a full stop in its place.
feedback.feed_forward: When both sides are complete, add a joining word or split the sentence.

items.decision_cue: and however it kept

payload.context: From a draft paragraph on local newspapers.
payload.sentence: The paper cut its print run, and however it kept the Sunday edition.
reasons: two joining words are doing one job
the two ideas do not belong in one sentence
the comma is missing
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: And has already made the join and however has already marked the turn. Whichever one you keep, the other has nothing left to do.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep one joining word per join and delete the spare.

payload.prompt_text: A town has put recycling bins on every street and the amount of waste sent for burning has not changed. Write one sentence that holds both facts together and shows how they sit with each other.

feedback.why_key: Both facts are true at once and the second disappoints the first, which is exactly the job one of these four words does.
feedback.feed_forward: Pick the joining word before you start writing the second half.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on free city transport. Find two short sentences standing next to each other and join them into one, choosing the word that shows how they relate. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: A page of short sentences reads as a list. One join, made on purpose, turns two facts into an argument.
feedback.feed_forward: Join two sentences only when you can name the relation between them.

points.title: Telling a piece of a sentence apart from a whole one

point_json.grammar_name: Main clauses, subordinate clauses, and what makes a fragment

teach.can_do: I can tell whether a group of words can stand alone as a sentence or needs to lean on another one.
teach.why_it_matters: Nearly every broken sentence in a written answer is one of these two pieces being used as if it were the other.
teach.meaning: A clause is a group of words with a subject and its own verb: the fare rose. That is the smallest thing English accepts as a sentence, and a clause that stands on its own like that is called a main clause. Now put one small word in front of it — because, although, when, if — and it can no longer stand up. It still has its subject and its verb, but it now leans on a main clause and cannot be left alone with a full stop after it. That leaning kind is called a subordinate clause.

form.pattern: main clause = subject + verb, able to stand alone. subordinate clause = joining word + subject + verb, unable to stand alone.
notes: The joining word is what makes the difference, not the length. Because it rained is short and still cannot stand alone.
A subordinate clause can come first or second: because the road flooded, the coach was late — or — the coach was late because the road flooded.
When it comes first, a comma marks where it ends. When it comes second, usually no comma is needed.
One sentence needs exactly one main clause. It may have none, one or several subordinate clauses hanging off it.
form.negative: Both kinds go negative in the ordinary way: although the road was not flooded, the coach was still late.
form.question: Ask of any group of words: could I put a full stop after this and walk away?

spec.caption: Both have a subject and a verb. Only one of them can be left alone with a full stop.

worked_example.sentence: Although the college added an evening class, the waiting list did not get any shorter.
worked_example.why_this_form: Although turns the first clause into the leaning kind, so the sentence still needs the second clause to stand on. The comma shows where the leaning part stops.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Delete although and you have two clauses that can each stand alone, and a comma between them is no longer enough to hold them together.

notice_set.sentence: Because the grant was withdrawn.
notice_set.question: Could this be a sentence on its own?
notice_set.why: It has a subject and a verb, but because leaves it leaning on something that never arrives.

notice_set.sentence: The grant was withdrawn.
notice_set.question: Could this be a sentence on its own?
notice_set.why: Subject, verb, and nothing in front of it asking for more. That is a whole sentence.

notice_set.sentence: When the results came out, half the class had already left.
notice_set.question: How many clauses are in this sentence?
notice_set.why: Two subjects and two verbs, joined by when. One of them leans and one of them stands.

notice_set.sentence: The results came out. Half the class had already left.
notice_set.question: Is anything broken here?
options: Yes, one part cannot stand alone
No, both parts are whole sentences
notice_set.why: Nothing is leaning, so two full stops are perfectly correct. It simply does not tell you how the two facts relate.

notice_set.sentence: Which explains why the scheme was quietly dropped.
notice_set.question: Could this be a sentence on its own?
notice_set.why: Which is a joining word too, so this piece is still waiting to be attached to whatever it explains.

notice_set.sentence: Fewer students took physics last year, although the department had opened two new labs.
notice_set.question: Which part could stand alone?
notice_set.why: The second part has although in front of it, so it leans. Cover it and the first part is still a sentence.

discovery.prompt: Every group of words on the left can be a sentence. None of the ones on the right can, even though all of them have a subject and a verb. What has been done to them?
pairs: the ferry stopped running
because the ferry stopped running
the tunnel was widened in 2018
when the tunnel was widened in 2018
the fee was reduced
although the fee was reduced

candidate_rules.text: One extra word at the front takes away the clause's ability to stand alone.
The ones on the right are about reasons and times, and reasons and times are never sentences.
A group of words cannot stand alone if it begins with because, when or although.

teach.rule_line: Could I put a full stop after this and walk away? If not, it is leaning on something.
teach.false_rule: That a long group of words is a sentence and a short one is not. Length has nothing to do with it: I agree is a sentence, and although the entire scheme was funded from the outset is not.

errors.wrong: Because the tuition fee rose again in September. Many applicants withdrew.
errors.right: Because the tuition fee rose again in September, many applicants withdrew.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner puts the full stop where they would take a breath, and the first piece is long enough to feel finished. Nothing in it sounds incomplete until you cover the piece that follows.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one mark: the full stop becomes a comma.

errors.wrong: The department opened two new labs, fewer students took physics.
errors.right: Although the department opened two new labs, fewer students took physics.
errors.why_it_happens: Both facts are true and they clearly belong together, so a comma feels like enough. Making one of them lean is the move the learner has never been shown.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: although.

errors.wrong: The lab was refitted over the summer the equipment arrived in October.
errors.right: The lab was refitted over the summer, and the equipment arrived in October.
errors.why_it_happens: Two clauses were written straight through without the writer noticing there was a seam. There is no punctuation error to see, which is why proofreading rarely catches it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: and.

errors.wrong: Despite the department opened two new labs, applications fell.
errors.right: Although the department opened two new labs, applications fell.
errors.why_it_happens: Despite and although both signal that a turn is coming, so they feel interchangeable. Nobody has told the learner that only one of the two can have a subject and a verb after it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: despite becomes although.

pays_in.note: Every complex sentence you will ever write is these two pieces in some arrangement.
pays_in.model: Although the fee was reduced, the number of applications barely moved.

pays_in.note: A long passage sentence unpacks the moment you find the clause that stands alone.
pays_in.model: Because funding was tied to enrolment, departments that shrank lost staff twice over.

pays_in.note: Part 3 answers need reasons attached to claims, not listed after them.
pays_in.model: People commute less because the cost has gone up, not because they prefer being at home.

used_in.quote: The prompt invites a concession in every paragraph, and a concession is a leaning clause.
Several sentences in the passage carry three clauses, and only one of them is the claim being made.

payload.sentence: Although the college kept the evening class open.
payload.question: Is this a complete sentence?
options: Only if you add a comma

feedback.why_key: Although leaves the clause waiting for the part it leans on, and that part never comes.
feedback.feed_forward: Cover the first word and see whether what is left could stand alone.

payload.sentence: The coach was late because the road flooded.
payload.question: How many of these two clauses could stand alone?

feedback.why_key: The coach was late stands up on its own. Because the road flooded leans on it and cannot be left by itself.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the clauses first, then ask which one is leaning.

items.decision_cue: Because the fee rose again in September.

payload.context: From a first draft about tuition costs.
payload.sentence: Because the fee rose again in September. Applications from mature students fell by a fifth.
reasons: the first piece cannot stand alone
the second piece cannot stand alone
the two pieces are unrelated
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The first piece has a subject and a verb, but because leaves it leaning, and a full stop gives it nothing to lean on.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a piece on its own before you put a full stop after it.

payload.context: Two facts about a college course, to be put into one sentence.
payload.stem: ___ the fee was reduced, the number of applications did not change.

feedback.why_key: One word at the front turns a stand-alone clause into a leaning one, and the comma then shows where the leaning part ends.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the joining word to the clause you want to lean.

payload.context: From a report on a rural bus route.
payload.stem: The 4.15 service was withdrawn in January, ___ the village has had no evening link since.

feedback.why_key: Both halves stand alone, so the comma needs a joining word beside it before the sentence will hold together.
feedback.feed_forward: Two stand-alone clauses need a joining word, not just a comma.

payload.context: Build one sentence in which the leaning clause comes first.

expected: because the reservoir was already low the ban came in early

feedback.why_key: The leaning clause comes first and hands over to a clause that can stand alone. Without that second clause the sentence never finishes.
feedback.feed_forward: After a leaning clause, always finish with one that stands alone.

payload.given: The library extended its opening hours. Very few students came in after eight.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence in which the first fact leans on the second.

expected: the library extended its opening hours very few students came in after eight
the library extended its opening hours, very few students came in after eight

feedback.why_key: Although turns a stand-alone clause into a leaning one, and the sentence then needs the second clause to hold it up.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the joining word in front of the clause you want to lean.

payload.audio_text: When we'd finished the audit, the office was already shut.

expected: when we'd finished the audit the office was already shut
when we had finished the audit the office was already shut
when wed finished the audit the office was already shut

feedback.why_key: When is the word doing all the work, and in speech it is short and unstressed. Miss it and you write two sentences the speaker never said.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small word at the start that makes a clause lean.

items.decision_cue: in September. Applications

payload.sentence: Because the fee rose again in September. Applications from mature students fell by a fifth.

feedback.why_key: One mark is wrong. The leaning clause has to be tied to the clause that follows it, not fenced off from it.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace the full stop after a leaning clause with a comma.

items.decision_cue: over the summer the equipment

payload.context: From a draft report on a college refit.
payload.sentence: The lab was refitted over the summer the equipment arrived in October.
reasons: two stand-alone clauses have been run together with nothing between them
the first clause cannot stand alone
the second clause cannot stand alone
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Both halves could take a full stop, and nothing at all has been put between them, so the reader has to find the seam unaided.
feedback.feed_forward: Put a joining word or a full stop at every seam between stand-alone clauses.

items.decision_cue: Because the river level dropped

payload.context: Two lines taken from different drafts of the same survey report.
sentences: Because the river level dropped, the survey was postponed.
The river level dropped. The survey was postponed.
meanings: The sentence states that the drop is why the survey moved.
Two facts are reported and the reader is left to guess how they connect.

feedback.why_key: A leaning clause puts the relation on the page. Two separate sentences leave the relation in the writer's head.
feedback.feed_forward: Use a leaning clause when the relation matters as much as the facts.

payload.prompt_text: A school has made an hour of exercise compulsory every day, and the timetable has lost an hour of science. Write one sentence in which one of those facts leans on the other.

feedback.why_key: Putting one fact into a leaning clause tells the reader which of the two you think is the news.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide which fact is the news, then make the other one lean.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on daily school exercise. Check every full stop: could what comes before it stand alone? Rewrite the two weakest sentences. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: This one check catches both of the errors that make a reader go back a line: a piece used as a whole, and two wholes glued with a comma.
feedback.feed_forward: Check every full stop before you check anything else.

points.title: Pinning one event to another with when, while, before, after and until

point_json.grammar_name: Time clauses: when, while, as, before, after, until, as soon as

teach.can_do: I can attach a time clause to a sentence and keep the verb inside it in the right form.
teach.why_it_matters: Time clauses are where will turns up and should not, and where a whole sentence quietly loses the part that can stand alone.
teach.meaning: A time clause is a leaning clause whose joining word answers when. When, while, as, before, after, until and as soon as each fix the second event against the first: at the same moment, earlier, later, or right up to a point and no further. Because the clause leans, it always travels with a clause that stands. And there is one habit here that catches everybody: when the whole sentence is about the future, the time clause itself stays in the present.

form.pattern: when / while / as / before / after / until / as soon as + subject + verb, + main clause
notes: Future meaning, present form: I will call you when the results arrive — never when the results will arrive.
While and as suit an activity that was already running; when suits a single moment.
Until means right up to a point and stops there: we waited until the last train left.
The time clause can go first or second. A comma is needed only when it goes first.
form.negative: The clause goes negative in the ordinary way: while the office was not open, deliveries were left at the gate.
form.question: Questions ask about the main clause, not the time clause: what did you do while the line was down?

spec.caption: Each joining word pins the second event to a different place against the first.

worked_example.sentence: We will move the servers as soon as the new room is ready.
worked_example.why_this_form: The whole sentence is about the future and the main clause already says so. The time clause takes the present because the future has been stated once and does not need saying twice.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: As soon as the new room will be ready is not a stronger or a politer version. It is simply not English, and it is one of the most visible errors at this level.

notice_set.sentence: As soon as the survey closed, the figures were published.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: As soon as puts the second event immediately after the first, with nothing in between.

notice_set.sentence: While the line was closed, the freight went by road.
notice_set.question: Did the freight move during the closure or after it?
notice_set.why: While covers a stretch of time, and the second event sits inside that stretch.

notice_set.sentence: The office had emptied before the storm reached the coast.
notice_set.question: Was anyone still in the office when the storm arrived?
notice_set.why: Before puts the emptying earlier, so the storm found the office already empty.

notice_set.sentence: I will send the file when the meeting ends.
notice_set.question: Is the meeting over?
notice_set.why: Ends looks like a present form, but the sentence is about the future. The time clause simply does not repeat it.

notice_set.sentence: We stayed until the last bus had gone.
notice_set.question: Did they leave before the last bus?
notice_set.why: Until marks the point at which the staying stopped, so they were still there when the bus went.

teach.rule_line: In a sentence about the future, the time clause stays in the present.
teach.false_rule: That every clause in a sentence about the future needs will. English states the future once, in the main clause, and the time clause does not repeat it.

errors.wrong: I will let you know as soon as the results will arrive.
errors.right: I will let you know as soon as the results arrive.
errors.why_it_happens: The sentence really is about the future and the learner is being consistent, which is exactly the reasoning that produces it. Nothing in the usual teaching says the time clause is the one place where consistency is wrong.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.

errors.wrong: After the depot closed in March. The drivers were moved to Ashfield.
errors.right: After the depot closed in March, the drivers were moved to Ashfield.
errors.why_it_happens: The time clause is long enough to feel like a finished thought, and after is not heard as a word that leaves anything hanging.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one mark: the full stop becomes a comma.

errors.wrong: When the alarm went off, everyone is outside within a minute.
errors.right: When the alarm went off, everyone was outside within a minute.
errors.why_it_happens: The two clauses are chosen one at a time and nobody reads the sentence as a single unit. The main clause slips back to the form the learner uses most.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is becomes was.

errors.wrong: We waited when the last train left.
errors.right: We waited until the last train left.
errors.why_it_happens: When and until both point at a moment and when is far commoner, so it arrives first. When names the moment something happened; until names the moment something stopped.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: when becomes until.

pays_in.note: A two-minute story is a chain of events, and time clauses are the links.
pays_in.model: While we were waiting for the parts to arrive, the whole line stood idle.

pays_in.note: Predictions almost always need a moment attached, and that is where will doubles up.
pays_in.model: Employers will only change their hiring once the shortage starts costing them contracts.

pays_in.note: An instruction in a talk is often a time clause, and the answer sits inside it.
pays_in.model: Before you submit the form, check that the reference number matches the letter.

used_in.quote: Any answer about what will happen next needs a moment pinned to it, and the extra will appears there every time.
Two of the answers are inside time clauses, and the speaker gives the moment before the fact.

payload.sentence: While the shop was being refitted, the staff worked from the unit next door.
payload.question: Where were the staff during the refit?

feedback.why_key: While covers the whole stretch of the refit, and the second clause tells you what filled it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read while as during the whole of that.

payload.sentence: The system will switch to the new server when the tests finish.

points.title: Choosing the right word to attach a reason or a result

point_json.grammar_name: Reason and result: because, since, as, so, therefore, consequently

teach.can_do: I can attach a reason or a result to a sentence with the right kind of word, in the right place.
teach.why_it_matters: These words look interchangeable and are not: one joins two clauses, one starts a new sentence, and mixing them is where comma splices come from.
teach.meaning: Cause and effect can be written from either end: name the reason, or name the result. English gives you three different kinds of word for it and they are not swappable. Because, since and as go in front of a clause and make it lean; they introduce the reason. So goes between two clauses that both stand; it introduces the result. Therefore and consequently are not joining words at all — they are adverbs, and they need a full stop in front of them.

form.pattern: reason: because / since / as + clause. result: main clause + , so + clause. adverb: full stop + Therefore, + clause.
notes: Because introduces the reason and so introduces the result. They face in opposite directions and you never need both.
Since and as also mean because, but they suit a reason the reader already knows.
Therefore and consequently cannot hold two clauses together. Put a full stop in front and a comma after.
form.negative: The reason clause goes negative as usual: because the funding was not renewed, the class closed at half term.
form.question: Ask which half is the reason and which is the result before you choose the word.

spec.caption: One arrow, two ways to write it. The word you choose depends on which end you are standing at.

worked_example.sentence: Because the funding was withdrawn in April, the evening class closed at half term.
worked_example.why_this_form: The withdrawal is the reason, and because is the word that puts a reason into a leaning clause. The comma marks where the leaning part ends.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: So in that slot would claim the withdrawal was the result of the closure, which turns the whole sentence round.

notice_set.sentence: The bridge was closed for repairs, so the diversion added twenty minutes.
notice_set.question: Which part is the result?
notice_set.why: So always introduces the result, and the result always comes second.

notice_set.sentence: Because the diversion added twenty minutes, the school bus arrived late.
notice_set.question: Which part is the reason?
notice_set.why: Because always introduces the reason, and here the reason has been put first.

notice_set.sentence: The rent rose again in March. Therefore, two of the shops did not renew.
notice_set.question: Could that full stop be a comma instead?
notice_set.why: Therefore is an adverb, not a joining word, so it cannot hold two clauses together across a comma.

notice_set.sentence: As the site had no drainage, the first winter flooded it.
notice_set.question: Does as mean at the same time here, or because?
notice_set.why: As has both meanings. The reason reading is the natural one when the second clause is plainly a consequence.

notice_set.sentence: Since the depot moved, the village has lost its only employer.
notice_set.question: Is since about time here, or about a reason?
notice_set.why: Since is genuinely ambiguous here, and that ambiguity is a good reason to write because when the reason is the point.

notice_set.sentence: The line was single track, so trains could not pass each other.
notice_set.question: Is the second clause the cause or the effect?
notice_set.why: After so, you are always reading an effect. Nothing else can follow it.

discovery.prompt: Each pair says the same thing twice. Work out what has to change when the word changes.
pairs: Because the fare rose, fewer people travelled.
The fare rose, so fewer people travelled.
Because the mill shut, the village lost its shop.
The mill shut, so the village lost its shop.
Because the survey was late, the report missed its date.
The survey was late, so the report missed its date.

candidate_rules.text: Because goes in front of the reason and so goes in front of the result, so the two clauses swap places.
Because goes at the start of a sentence and so goes in the middle of one.
Use because when the sentence is about the past and so when it is about the present.

teach.rule_line: Because points at the reason. So points at the result. Therefore needs a full stop.
teach.false_rule: That because, so and therefore are three ways of writing one word. They are three different grammatical classes and they sit in three different places.

contrast.question: Am I about to write the reason or the result?

fork.answer: The reason, and I want it in a leaning clause
fork.selects: because, since or as in front of the clause

fork.answer: The result, and both halves are staying as full clauses
fork.selects: so between them, after a comma

fork.answer: The result, and I want a fresh sentence for it
fork.selects: a full stop, then therefore or consequently

a.text: The evening class closed because the funding ran out.
a.means: The money went first. The closure is what followed from it.

b.text: The evening class closed, so the funding ran out.
b.means: The closure came first, and losing the money is what followed from that.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote so. That tells your reader the closure came first and the money went because of it. The facts are unchanged and the arrow has been turned round, which is far harder to spot than a broken form.

edge_case.text: As and since also mean because, and as also means at the same time. In a timed answer that ambiguity costs you nothing if you simply write because whenever the reason is the point.

contrast.stronger_test: Say the two halves out loud with and because of that between them. Whichever half sits second is the result, and that is the half so belongs in front of.

worked_pairs.a: Rents rose sharply, so two of the independent shops did not renew.
worked_pairs.b: Rents rose sharply because two of the independent shops did not renew.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: so two of the independent shops did not renew
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: because two of the independent shops did not renew
worked_pairs.gloss: The first blames the rents for the closures. The second blames the closures for the rents, and that is a different town.

worked_pairs.a: The path floods every winter, so the council has fenced it off.
worked_pairs.b: Because the path floods every winter, the council has fenced it off.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: so the council has fenced it off
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: Because the path floods every winter
worked_pairs.gloss: Same arrow, two ways of writing it. The second puts the reason first, which leaves the fencing as the news.

worked_pairs.a: The line was never electrified. Therefore, journey times have not moved since the 1980s.
worked_pairs.b: The line was never electrified, so journey times have not moved since the 1980s.
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct. The first is two sentences and reads formally; the second is one and reads plainly. What you may never do is put therefore where so is.

errors.wrong: The rent rose again in March, therefore two of the shops did not renew.
errors.right: The rent rose again in March. Therefore, two of the shops did not renew.
errors.why_it_happens: Therefore means what so means, so it feels as though it can stand in the same place. Nobody has told the learner that meaning and grammatical class are two separate facts about a word.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one mark: the comma becomes a full stop.

errors.wrong: Because the mill shut, so the village lost its only shop.
errors.right: Because the mill shut, the village lost its only shop.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner marks the relation twice to be certain the reader sees it. Both words are correct on their own and in English exactly one of them has to go.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: so.
errors.l1_note: Marking the pair on both clauses is the standard pattern in several Asian languages.

errors.wrong: The evening class closed, so the funding ran out.
errors.right: The evening class closed because the funding ran out.
errors.why_it_happens: Under time pressure the learner writes the two facts in the order they thought of them and reaches for the commonest joining word. So then quietly reverses the cause and the effect without breaking anything.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: so becomes because.

errors.wrong: Because of the funding was withdrawn, the class closed.
errors.right: Because the funding was withdrawn, the class closed.
errors.why_it_happens: Because of is stored as one unit and comes out whole. It takes a noun, not a clause, and here a clause with its own subject and verb has been put after it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: of.

points.title: Admitting a fact that works against you and still keeping your point

point_json.grammar_name: Contrast clauses: although, even though, though, while, whereas

teach.can_do: I can put a fact that works against my point inside the same sentence and still keep my point.
teach.why_it_matters: Conceding something and then holding your ground is the shape of a strong body paragraph, and it is one leaning clause away.
teach.meaning: Sometimes two facts are both true and one of them makes the other surprising. Although, even though, though, while and whereas put the surprising fact into a leaning clause, so the reader knows immediately which of the two you are actually arguing for: the main clause always wins. Whereas is slightly different from the rest. It sets two things side by side and compares them, rather than admitting one in order to keep the other.

form.pattern: although / even though / though / while / whereas + clause, + main clause
notes: The main clause is the one you mean. The leaning clause is the fact you are giving away.
Even though is the strong version of although; though is the informal one and often comes at the end in speech.
Whereas compares two different subjects: online sales rose, whereas footfall fell.
One contrast word per sentence. Although at the front and but in the middle is one too many.
form.negative: The leaning clause takes its negative in the ordinary way: although the trial did not finish, the results were published.
form.question: Ask which of the two facts you want your reader to walk away with. That one goes in the main clause.

left.role: the concession, in the leaning clause

right.role: the point you are making, in the main clause
right.text: very few people kept it past a week

spec.caption: Both facts are true. The one in the main clause is the one you are arguing for.

worked_example.sentence: Although the app was free to download, very few people kept it past the first week.
worked_example.why_this_form: The free download is the fact that works against the point, so it goes into the leaning clause and the abandonment is left standing as the news.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Swap the two clauses over and the sentence becomes an argument for the app: the abandonment turns into a detail and the free download becomes the point.

notice_set.sentence: Although the tablets were handed out in September, the reading scores did not move.
notice_set.question: Which fact is the writer arguing for?
notice_set.why: The main clause carries the point; the leaning clause holds the fact being conceded.

notice_set.sentence: Even though the trial ran for three years, the findings were never published.
notice_set.question: Is three years a long time for this writer's argument?
options: Yes, and that is the job even though is doing
notice_set.why: Even though marks the concession as a strong one, which makes the main clause more surprising.

notice_set.sentence: Online sales rose by a fifth, whereas footfall in the shops fell.
notice_set.question: Are these two facts about the same thing?
options: No, two different things are being compared
notice_set.why: Whereas sets two subjects side by side rather than conceding one in order to keep the other.

notice_set.sentence: While the software was easy to install, the training took a fortnight.
notice_set.question: What does while mean here?
notice_set.why: While has a time meaning and a contrast meaning. Nothing here is happening at the same time, so only the contrast reading is available.

notice_set.sentence: The training took a fortnight, though the software installed in an hour.
notice_set.question: Where has the contrast word gone?
notice_set.why: Though is happy to sit in the middle, and in speech it will even come at the very end of the sentence.

teach.rule_line: The fact you are conceding goes in the leaning clause. Your point stays in the main one.
teach.false_rule: That although and but are two spellings of one word. Although makes a clause lean; but joins two clauses that both stand. Use one or the other, never both.

errors.wrong: Although the app was free, but almost nobody kept it.
errors.right: Although the app was free, almost nobody kept it.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner marks the turn twice so the reader cannot miss it, and in several languages that doubling is the correct pattern. In English one of the two words is always redundant.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: but.
errors.l1_note: The doubled pattern is standard in several South and East Asian languages.

errors.wrong: Although the high cost, the scheme went ahead.
errors.right: Although the cost was high, the scheme went ahead.
errors.why_it_happens: Although has been stored as a contrast word rather than as a clause word, so it is put in front of whatever the contrast is about. What follows here is a noun phrase with no verb in it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: was.

errors.wrong: Although the reading scores did not move, the tablets were handed out in September.
errors.right: Although the tablets were handed out in September, the reading scores did not move.
errors.why_it_happens: Both clauses are true, so the sentence sounds fine when it is read back. The learner has put the news in the leaning clause and the concession in the main one, and the argument now runs backwards.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: although goes in front of the other clause.

errors.wrong: The software installed in an hour, the training took a fortnight.
errors.right: Although the software installed in an hour, the training took a fortnight.
errors.why_it_happens: The contrast between the two facts is obvious to the writer, so it feels as though it has been stated. Nothing on the page states it, and a comma cannot hold two stand-alone clauses together.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: although.

pays_in.note: A paragraph that never concedes anything reads as if the other side was never considered.
pays_in.model: Although phones are a genuine distraction in class, a blanket ban moves the problem to the school gate.

pays_in.note: Part 3 rewards an answer that admits the obvious objection before answering it.
pays_in.model: Even though it costs more up front, you get the money back over about four years.

pays_in.note: The writer's real claim is always in the clause without the contrast word.
pays_in.model: While the scheme met its recycling target, the cost per tonne doubled.

used_in.quote: A discussion answer has to state the other view fairly before it disagrees, and that is a leaning clause.
The follow-up questions push for both sides, and the neat answer concedes one and keeps the other.

feedback.why_key: Though puts the longer shifts into the leaning clause, so the better pay is what the speaker is really saying.
feedback.feed_forward: The clause without the contrast word is the one that counts.

points.title: Deciding between despite and although by looking at what comes next

point_json.grammar_name: despite / in spite of + noun or -ing, versus although + clause

teach.can_do: I can choose between despite and although by looking at what I am about to write next.
teach.why_it_matters: Despite he was tired is one of the most common written errors at this level, and the fix is a question about the next four words, not about meaning.
teach.meaning: Despite, in spite of and although all mark the same turn, and almost no learner ever gets the meaning wrong. What goes wrong is the grammar on the right of the word. Although is a clause word: a subject and its verb must follow it. Despite and in spite of are prepositions: a noun, a pronoun or an -ing form must follow them, and never a subject with a verb. So the decision is not about what you mean at all. It is about what shape the next few words are going to take.

form.pattern: although + subject + verb ... | despite / in spite of + noun phrase or -ing form ...
notes: In spite of is three words and despite is one. There is no despite of.
To put a clause after despite you have to wrap it first: despite the fact that the cost rose. Correct, and four words longer than although.
Either can start the sentence or sit in the middle. The comma goes in only when the concession comes first.
form.negative: Negatives change nothing about the choice: although the funding was not renewed, or despite the loss of funding.
form.question: Ask what the word straight after the linker is going to be: a subject, or a noun?

left.role: although: a subject and a verb follow

right.role: despite: a noun or an -ing form follows

spec.caption: Same meaning, two different shapes on the right-hand side. The shape is the whole decision.

worked_example.sentence: Despite the rise in fuel duty, freight traffic on the motorway kept growing.
worked_example.why_this_form: What follows the linker is a noun phrase — the rise — with no verb of its own, and a noun phrase is exactly what despite takes.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Although the rise in fuel duty is not a milder version of the same sentence. It is an unfinished clause, and the reader waits for a verb that never arrives.

notice_set.sentence: Despite the heavy rain, the survey went ahead.
notice_set.question: What comes straight after despite?
notice_set.why: The heavy rain has no verb in it, so it is a noun phrase, and that is what despite requires.

notice_set.sentence: Although it rained heavily, the survey went ahead.
notice_set.question: What comes straight after although?
notice_set.why: It rained is a subject and its verb, which is exactly what although requires.

notice_set.sentence: Despite losing two days to the weather, the team finished the survey.
notice_set.question: What comes straight after despite?
notice_set.why: Losing is an -ing form, and despite takes those as happily as it takes nouns.

notice_set.sentence: Despite the fact that it rained for three days, the survey went ahead.
notice_set.question: Why is the fact there?
options: To make the sentence more formal
To give despite a noun to hold on to
notice_set.why: The fact is the noun despite needs, and the clause is then hung on it. Correct, and four words longer than although.

notice_set.sentence: Although the heavy rain, the survey went ahead.
notice_set.question: Is this a sentence?
notice_set.why: Although has been given a noun phrase and is still waiting for a verb, so the first clause never finishes.

notice_set.sentence: In spite of the delay, the results were published on time.
notice_set.question: Could despite replace in spite of here?
notice_set.why: They are the same word in two lengths and they take exactly the same thing after them.

discovery.prompt: All six sentences mean the same thing. Three of them are correct and three are not. Work out what the correct ones have in common.
pairs: Despite the delay, the results were published.
Despite the results were delayed, they were published.
Although the results were delayed, they were published.
Although the delay, the results were published.
Despite being delayed, the results were published.
Despite they were delayed, the results were published.

candidate_rules.text: Despite is followed by a noun or an -ing form; although is followed by a subject and a verb.
Despite is for short concessions and although is for long ones.
Use despite at the start of a sentence and although in the middle of one.

teach.rule_line: Look right, not left. A subject and verb means although; a noun means despite.
teach.false_rule: That despite is the formal word and although the ordinary one, so despite is the safer choice in an essay. They are equally formal. Only the shape after them differs.

contrast.question: Is a subject and a verb coming next, or a noun?

fork.answer: A subject and its verb: the cost rose, they were delayed
A noun phrase or an -ing form: the rising cost, being delayed

a.text: Despite the sharp rise in fares, passenger numbers held up.
a.means: Correct English. A noun phrase follows the linker, and a preposition is what a noun phrase needs.

b.text: Although the sharp rise in fares, passenger numbers held up.
b.means: Broken English. Although is left waiting for a verb that never arrives.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote although in front of a noun phrase. Your reader now waits for a verb, does not get one, and has to go back to find where the first clause was supposed to end. The meaning was never in doubt; the shape was.

edge_case.text: Despite can carry a clause if you give it a noun to hold first: despite the fact that the cost rose. It is correct, it is four words longer than although, and in a timed answer it is rarely worth the space.

contrast.stronger_test: Cover everything to the left of the linker and read the next four words. If they could start a sentence on their own, you need although. If they could not, you need despite.

worked_pairs.a: Despite the closure of the coast road, the ferry kept its timetable.
worked_pairs.b: Although the coast road was closed, the ferry kept its timetable.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: the closure of the coast road
worked_pairs.gloss: The same fact twice: once as a noun with no verb, once as a clause with one. The linker follows the shape, not the meaning.

worked_pairs.a: In spite of losing two days to the weather, the team finished on time.
worked_pairs.b: Even though they lost two days to the weather, the team finished on time.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: losing two days to the weather
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: they lost two days to the weather
worked_pairs.gloss: An -ing form has no subject of its own, so it takes the preposition. Give it a subject and it needs the clause word instead.

worked_pairs.a: Despite the fact that the grant was cut, the survey continued.
worked_pairs.b: Although the grant was cut, the survey continued.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: the fact that the grant was cut
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct. The fact that is the scaffolding that lets a preposition carry a clause, and it costs four words you did not have to spend.

errors.wrong: Despite the cost was high, the scheme went ahead.
errors.right: Although the cost was high, the scheme went ahead.
errors.why_it_happens: Despite and although mean the same thing, so the learner takes whichever comes to mind and never checks the shape of what follows. Meaning is doing the choosing, and meaning is not the deciding factor here.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: despite becomes although.
errors.l1_note: Very frequent where the first language uses one word for both.

errors.wrong: Although the high cost of the works, the scheme went ahead.
errors.right: Despite the high cost of the works, the scheme went ahead.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been told that although is the safe academic word and reaches for it first. Nothing then checks whether a verb is on its way.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: although becomes despite.

errors.wrong: Despite of the delay, the results were published on time.
errors.right: Despite the delay, the results were published on time.
errors.why_it_happens: In spite of ends in of and despite does not. The two are stored as one item with an of floating loose inside it, and the of surfaces in the wrong half.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: of.

errors.wrong: Despite the delay, but the results were published on time.
errors.right: Despite the delay, the results were published on time.
errors.why_it_happens: The turn feels as though it needs marking on both sides of the comma, and in several first languages it genuinely does.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: but.

points.title: Saying why something was done, and choosing between to and so that

point_json.grammar_name: Purpose: to, in order to, so as to, so that

teach.can_do: I can say why something was done, and pick the right shape depending on who does the second thing.
teach.why_it_matters: For to improve and for improving are among the most stubborn errors at this level, and the fix is one question about who does what.
teach.meaning: A purpose answers why. English has two shapes for it and the choice between them is mechanical. If the same person does both things, the second one goes into a bare to-infinitive: the council widened the path to slow the cyclists down. If somebody else does the second thing, a to-infinitive has nowhere to put that new subject, so you need so that and a full clause: the council widened the path so that walkers could pass safely. The deciding question is not formality. It is whether the subject changes.

form.pattern: same subject: main clause + to / in order to / so as to + verb. different subject: main clause + so that + subject + verb.
notes: In order to and so as to are the formal versions of to. They add no meaning at all.
The clause after so that almost always carries can, could, will or would.
For + -ing says what a thing is for, not why somebody acted: this valve is for releasing pressure.
form.negative: The negative purpose is so as not to or in order not to: we left early so as not to miss the last bus.
form.question: Ask who does the second action. The same person means to; a different person means so that.

left.text: the clinic opened on Saturdays to reach shift workers

right.text: the clinic opened on Saturdays so that shift workers could attend

spec.caption: Who does the second action decides the shape. Nothing else does.

worked_example.sentence: The clinic began opening on Saturdays so that shift workers could see a nurse without losing pay.
worked_example.why_this_form: The clinic opens and the shift workers do the seeing. Two different subjects, so the purpose needs a clause of its own with could inside it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: To see a nurse would attach the seeing to the clinic, and the sentence would end up claiming the clinic wanted to be examined.

notice_set.sentence: The council widened the path to slow the cyclists down.
notice_set.question: Who slows the cyclists down?
notice_set.why: A to-infinitive has no subject of its own, so it borrows the one standing in front of it.

notice_set.sentence: The council widened the path so that walkers could pass safely.
notice_set.question: Who passes safely?
notice_set.why: So that opens a full clause with its own subject, which is exactly why the subject is allowed to change.

notice_set.sentence: The hospital extended its opening hours to reduce the queue.
notice_set.question: Could so that replace to here without changing the meaning?
options: Yes, if a subject is added
notice_set.why: So that the queue would be shorter says the same thing in more words. Both are correct; to is shorter.

notice_set.sentence: We left an hour early so as not to miss the ferry.
notice_set.question: What does so as not to mean here?
options: We wanted to avoid missing it
notice_set.why: So as not to is the standard negative purpose, and it is what keeps for not missing off the page.

notice_set.sentence: This valve is for releasing pressure.
notice_set.question: Is this a purpose clause?
options: Yes, it says why somebody did something
No, it says what a thing is for
notice_set.why: For plus -ing describes a function. It cannot say why an action was taken.

notice_set.sentence: The trust bought two vans in order to reach the outlying villages.
notice_set.question: How does in order to differ from plain to here?
options: It is more formal, and nothing else
It changes who does the reaching
notice_set.why: In order to is a longer, more formal to. It adds no meaning whatsoever.

discovery.prompt: Three of these six are correct and three are not. Work out what the correct ones have in common.

The clinic opened late so that shift workers could attend.

candidate_rules.text: To takes a bare verb when the subject stays the same; so that takes a full clause when the subject changes.
For plus an -ing form is always wrong after a main clause.
Use to in short sentences and so that in long ones.

teach.rule_line: Same person doing both things? Use to. A different person? Use so that.
teach.false_rule: That for plus an -ing form is the way to say why. For plus -ing says what something is for. Why somebody acted needs to or so that.

contrast.question: Does the same person do both actions?

fork.answer: Yes — one subject does both of them
fork.selects: to, in order to or so as to, plus a bare verb

fork.answer: No — somebody else does the second one
fork.selects: so that plus a full clause, usually with can or could

a.means: The clinic does the seeing. It wanted a bigger caseload.

b.text: The clinic opened on Saturdays so that more patients could be seen.
b.means: The patients are the ones who get seen. The clinic did it for them.

minimal_pair.only_difference: to see / so that ... could be seen

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote to see more patients. That hands the seeing to the clinic and turns a service into an ambition. If the people you are writing about are the ones who benefit, the purpose needs a subject of its own.

edge_case.text: So that will drop its that in speech, and in order that survives in very formal writing. Neither changes the decision, which is only ever about whether the subject stays the same.

contrast.stronger_test: Put a subject in front of the second verb and see whether it is the same one as the first. If you had to write a new subject, you have to write so that.

worked_pairs.a: The trust bought two vans to reach the outlying villages.
worked_pairs.b: The trust bought two vans so that the outlying villages could be reached.

worked_pairs.gloss: In the first the trust does the reaching. In the second the villages are reached, and the sentence needs a clause to say so.

worked_pairs.a: The council fenced the path to keep walkers off the cliff edge.

worked_pairs.b: We left an hour early so that the children would not miss the ferry.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: so that the children would not miss
worked_pairs.gloss: The negative works the same way. As soon as the subject changes, the infinitive cannot carry it and a clause has to.

errors.right: The clinic opened on Saturdays to reach shift workers.

errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: for reaching becomes to reach.
errors.l1_note: Almost universal where the first language uses one preposition for purpose.

points.title: Saying how much of something there was and what it led to

point_json.grammar_name: Degree and result: so ... that, such ... that, too ... to, enough ... to

teach.can_do: I can say that there was so much of something that it produced a result, or so much that it blocked one.
teach.why_it_matters: It turns a bare adjective into a claim with a consequence attached, which is the difference between describing a problem and arguing about one.
teach.meaning: Very tells your reader the amount. So, such, too and enough tell them what the amount did. So and such report an amount that produced a result: the hall was so cold that half the class went home. Too reports an amount that blocked one: the hall was too cold to sit in, and nobody sat in it. Enough reports an amount that was sufficient, and the result did happen. Choosing between them is not about strength of feeling. It is about whether the thing happened or not.

form.pattern: so + adjective / adverb + that + clause | such + a / an + adjective + noun + that + clause | too + adjective + to + verb | adjective + enough + to + verb | enough + noun + to + verb
notes: So goes in front of an adjective or an adverb. Such goes in front of a noun phrase: so cold, but such a cold hall.
Enough goes after an adjective and in front of a noun: warm enough, but enough chairs.
Too and enough take a bare to-infinitive with no that: too cold to sit in, warm enough to sit in.
So and such take a full clause after that, and in speech the that is often dropped.
form.negative: Too already carries a negative result, so the clause after it stays positive: it was too cold to sit in, never too cold not to sit in.
form.question: Did the thing happen? If it did not, the sentence needs too.

spec.label: how much, and what the amount did

steps.text: not enough space to seat them
steps.gloss: there was too little, so it did not happen
there was too much of the wrong thing, so it did not happen
the amount was sufficient, and it happened

worked_example.sentence: The lecture hall was so cold that a third of the group left before the break.
worked_example.why_this_form: Something did happen because of the cold, and the sentence names it. So plus that is the shape for an amount that produced a result.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Too cold to stay would say that nobody stayed at all. The cold would have blocked the sitting rather than merely driving some people out.

notice_set.sentence: The hall was too small to take the whole year group.
notice_set.question: Did the whole year group fit in?
notice_set.why: Too always reports something that did not happen. The size is what stopped it.

notice_set.sentence: The hall was small enough to heat on one boiler.
notice_set.question: Was one boiler enough?
notice_set.why: Enough reports an amount that was sufficient, and what follows it did happen.

notice_set.sentence: The reading list was so long that most students never finished it.
notice_set.question: Did anyone finish it?
notice_set.why: So plus that reports a result that really happened, and most is not all.

notice_set.sentence: It was such a long reading list that most students never finished it.
notice_set.question: What is different from the sentence before?
options: Only the shape, because the adjective now sits in front of a noun
notice_set.why: Such is what you use when the adjective has a noun attached to it. The claim is unchanged.

notice_set.sentence: There were not enough chairs to seat the whole group.
notice_set.question: Did everyone get a chair?
notice_set.why: Enough in front of a noun counts the things, and not enough says the count fell short.

discovery.prompt: Each pair uses the same adjective about the same hall. Work out what changes between the left and the right.
pairs: The hall was too small to take the year group.
The hall was small enough to heat on one boiler.
The list was too long to finish in a term.
The list was so long that most students never finished it.
It was too cold to sit through the lecture.
It was so cold that a third of them left early.

candidate_rules.text: On the left the amount stopped it happening; on the right something did happen.
Too is used for bad things and enough for good ones.
Too goes with an infinitive and so goes with that, so the shape decides the meaning.

teach.rule_line: Did it happen? If it did not, you need too. If it did, you need so, such or enough.
teach.false_rule: That too is simply a stronger very. Very reports an amount and claims nothing else. Too reports that the amount stopped something from happening.

contrast.question: Did it happen, or did the amount stop it happening?

fork.answer: It happened, and I want to say how striking the cause was
fork.selects: so + adjective + that, or such + a + noun + that

fork.answer: It did not happen: there was too much of something in the way
It happened because there was as much as was needed
fork.selects: adjective + enough + to, or enough + noun + to

a.text: The hall was too small to heat on one boiler.
a.means: One boiler was not used, because the size ruled it out.

b.text: The hall was small enough to heat on one boiler.
b.means: One boiler was used, and the size is exactly why it worked.

minimal_pair.only_difference: too small to / small enough to

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote too small to heat on one boiler. That says the heating never happened and blames the size for it, which is the opposite of what you meant. Too always reports a failure, whatever the adjective in front of it.

edge_case.text: Enough goes after an adjective and in front of a noun: warm enough, but enough chairs. It is the one placement rule in this area and it catches everybody exactly once.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask whether the thing actually took place. If it did not, the sentence needs too. If it did, it needs so, such or enough, and nothing else will do.

worked_pairs.a: The reading list was too long to finish in one term.
worked_pairs.b: The reading list was so long that most students never finished it.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: so long that most students never finished it
worked_pairs.gloss: The first says nobody finished it, as a matter of arithmetic. The second says most did not, as a matter of fact, and leaves room for the ones who did.

worked_pairs.a: It was so cold in the hall that a third of them left early.
worked_pairs.b: It was such a cold hall that a third of them left early.
worked_pairs.gloss: Identical claims. So sits in front of a bare adjective; such sits in front of an adjective with a noun behind it.

worked_pairs.a: There were not enough places to take everyone who applied.
worked_pairs.b: There were too few places to take everyone who applied.
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct and both report the same shortfall. Not enough counts up from nothing; too few counts down from what was needed.

errors.wrong: The hall was enough warm to work in all afternoon.
errors.right: The hall was warm enough to work in all afternoon.
errors.why_it_happens: Every other word of this kind goes in front of the adjective — very warm, too warm, quite warm — so enough is put there too. It is the one that goes behind.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: enough goes after warm.

errors.wrong: It was so a cold hall that a third of them left early.
errors.right: It was such a cold hall that a third of them left early.
errors.why_it_happens: So is the commoner word and it has already been learned as the degree word. Nothing in the way it is taught says that a noun after the adjective switches it to such.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: so becomes such.

errors.wrong: The reading list was too long that most students never finished it.
errors.right: The reading list was so long that most students never finished it.
errors.why_it_happens: Too and so both report a striking amount, so they feel interchangeable, and that is dragged across from the so pattern. Too never takes that.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: too becomes so.

errors.wrong: The hall was too big to hold the whole year group, so everyone got a seat.
errors.right: The hall was big enough to hold the whole year group, so everyone got a seat.
errors.why_it_happens: Too is heard as a strong very and the writer means the size was impressive. The sentence then reports a failure in its first half and a success in its second.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: too big becomes big enough.

pays_in.note: It states a problem and its consequence in one sentence instead of two.
pays_in.model: Class sizes are now so large that a new teacher rarely learns every name in a term.

pays_in.note: It is the natural shape for the why part of a two-minute answer.
pays_in.model: The queue was so long that we gave up and went to the market instead.

pays_in.note: A True or False stem often turns on whether the passage said something happened or did not.
pays_in.model: The samples were too degraded to date accurately.

used_in.quote: The answer has to say what the shortage has actually produced, not simply that it is large.
Saying why you would recommend it is a degree and a result held together in one sentence.
